Advertising. The commercial practice of using media—print, radio, television, and later digital channels—to promote products and influence consumer behavior. As mass production created surplus goods in the early twentieth century, advertising evolved from simple notices into a sophisticated industry of persuasion.

Advertising emerged in modern form during the Industrial Revolution, when printed newspapers and magazines provided media for commercial messages. But scale was limited until mass circulation grew in the late eighteen hundreds. The real transformation came with the rise of department stores and packaged goods. Companies like Procter and Gamble pioneered brand-building through repeated commercial messaging. By the early twentieth century, advertising had professionalized into its own industry. Ad agencies like J. Walter Thompson and Ogilvy and Mather employed creative strategists who scientifically targeted demographics.

Print media—newspapers and magazines like The Saturday Evening Post—became dependent on advertising revenue. Advertisers gained enormous influence over editorial content and cultural messaging. Then radio in the nineteen twenties through forties and television from the nineteen fifties onward became advertising's primary vehicles. Sponsored programs and commercial breaks made broadcasting profitable and shaped the medium's content.

By mid-twentieth century, advertising became increasingly psychological. Advertisers studied consumer motivations and deployed Freudian imagery to link products to subconscious desires and status. Advertising created the concept of consumer culture—the notion that happiness and identity were purchasable commodities. It fundamentally transformed Americans from producers to consumers and normalized continuous consumption as a way of life. This advertising revolution became central to American capitalism, shaping culture, values, and consumption patterns while generating enormous wealth for publishers and ad agencies.
